title: Schema Design
subtitle: CREATE TABLE, data types, constraints, and normalization
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Before you can INSERT data, you need to define what structure it follows. Without a schema, every row could look different — there's no enforcement of types, required fields, or relationships.
whyItExists.solution: CREATE TABLE defines the table's columns, data types, and constraints. Constraints enforce rules: NOT NULL means the field can't be empty, UNIQUE prevents duplicates, FOREIGN KEY links tables together.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When building a new application or migrating data. Schema design is upfront work that saves huge amounts of pain later.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Schema-less (document) databases like MongoDB trade structure for flexibility — useful when data shape varies per row. For well-defined, relational data, SQL schemas are the right choice.

explainModes.beginner: CREATE TABLE is like defining a spreadsheet's columns before any data goes in. You say 'this column holds integers', 'that one holds text and can't be empty', 'this one must be unique.' The database then enforces those rules on every INSERT.
explainModes.simple: CREATE TABLE name (col1 TYPE constraint, col2 TYPE, ...);. Types: INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB (binary). Constraints: NOT NULL (required), UNIQUE (no duplicates), DEFAULT value, CHECK (custom rule), PRIMARY KEY (unique identifier), FOREIGN KEY (links to another table). ALTER TABLE adds/renames columns. DROP TABLE deletes it. IF NOT EXISTS prevents error if already exists.
explainModes.standard: SQLite type affinity: any column can store any type (flexible but different from PostgreSQL). INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in SQLite is an alias for the rowid (auto-increment). AUTOINCREMENT keyword prevents rowid reuse after deletion. FOREIGN KEY constraints must be enabled explicitly: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. CHECK constraint: CHECK (price > 0). ON DELETE CASCADE deletes child rows when parent is deleted. ON UPDATE CASCADE propagates updates.
explainModes.technical: SQLite's type system uses affinity (TEXT, NUMERIC, INTEGER, REAL, BLOB) — values are stored in the most efficient format. PostgreSQL has strict typing. Normalization levels: 1NF (atomic values, no repeating groups), 2NF (no partial dependencies), 3NF (no transitive dependencies). IDENTITY/SERIAL in PostgreSQL: CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY). Constraints can be named: CONSTRAINT pk_users PRIMARY KEY (id). Named constraints can be dropped: ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT constraint_name.
explainModes.deepDive: Normalization vs denormalization trade-off: normalized schemas minimize redundancy (single source of truth) but require joins; denormalized schemas (computed/duplicated columns) are faster to read but harder to keep consistent. The right level depends on read vs write ratio and query complexity. Temporal tables (PostgreSQL) track history. Partitioning (PostgreSQL) splits large tables by range or list — each partition is stored separately. Generated columns (PostgreSQL 12+, SQLite 3.31+): GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED — computed from other columns, stored on disk. Virtual generated columns are computed on read.

content.code:
-- Create the users table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name      TEXT    NOT NULL,
    email     TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    city      TEXT,
    joined_at TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT (DATE('now'))
);

-- Create the products table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS products (
    id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name     TEXT    NOT NULL,
    category TEXT    NOT NULL,
    price    REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),  -- no negative prices!
    stock    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock >= 0)
);

-- Create the orders table with FOREIGN KEY references
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (
    id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    user_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id)    ON DELETE CASCADE,
    product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    total      REAL    NOT NULL,
    ordered_at TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT (DATETIME('now'))
);

questions.question: What constraint ensures a column cannot contain NULL values?
questions.explanation: NOT NULL is the constraint that prevents a column from storing NULL. If you try to INSERT without providing a value for a NOT NULL column (and there's no DEFAULT), the database raises an error. UNIQUE only prevents duplicate values — it still allows multiple NULLs in most databases.

faq.q: What are the SQLite data types?
faq.a: SQLite uses 5 storage classes: NULL, INTEGER (1-8 bytes), REAL (8-byte float), TEXT (UTF-8), and BLOB (raw binary). Unlike PostgreSQL which is strictly typed, SQLite stores values in the most efficient format based on 'type affinity'. This means TEXT '42' and INTEGER 42 can both live in the same column.

faq.q: How do I enable foreign key enforcement in SQLite?
faq.a: By default, SQLite parses FOREIGN KEY syntax but doesn't enforce it. Run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; at the start of every connection. This is a per-connection setting — you must set it each time you open the database.
